title: Four proposed changes
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four ER teams, each with the same problem: volumes up, staffing flat, and a leadership team asking what AI will do about it. Each proposed one change.

**One of them will genuinely improve cycle time and genuinely weaken the record.** Find it, and notice that it is not the one that breaks a rule.

artifacts.label: Change A
artifacts.body: "A model drafts the investigation report from the investigator's notes, the interview summaries and the document list. The investigator edits the draft, adds the finding, and signs it. Piloted on 22 matters: median drafting time fell from 4.5 hours to 1.2, and median time-to-close fell 31%. Investigators describe the drafts as 'basically right, needs tightening.' Report quality reviews by the ER lead rate the drafted reports as better written than the previous baseline."

artifacts.label: Change B
artifacts.body: "Before the first interview in every misconduct matter, a model produces a document inventory: what exists in the systems the investigator can reach, what is referenced in the complaint but not present, and where two documents conflict. The investigator verifies each row against the source document before using it. Cycle time is unchanged and in complex matters slightly worse. The three matters that went to hearing during the pilot had no missing-evidence challenges, against two in the comparable prior period."

artifacts.label: Change C
artifacts.body: "At intake, a model classifies each matter as requiring formal investigation or suitable for informal resolution, applying the criteria in the ER handbook. A manager reviews the classification. The team measures routing consistency (how often two reviewers agree with the classification) which has risen from 71% to 94%. The team considers this the strongest evidence of improved fairness it has ever had."

artifacts.label: Change D
artifacts.body: "No AI. The closing template is rewritten so that the report cannot be submitted without a row for every allegation raised, each with its resolution, the evidence relied on, and (where an allegation could not be resolved) an explicit statement that it was not resolved and why. Median time-to-close rose by 1.5 days. In the first quarter, 19% of submitted reports came back for a missing allegation row."

reasoning:
**A is the answer, and every number in it is good.** That is what makes it the hardest one on the page. Drafting time down 73%, cycle time down 31%, a human edits and signs, quality reviews improved. Nothing in it is forbidden. Report drafting is not a rung-five determination; the investigator still reaches the finding.

And the record gets weaker anyway, in three ways that no metric in the pilot could see.

**The rung provenance is gone.** Module 4's whole argument is that the report is where a sentence's rung becomes visible or invisible. When a model composes the prose, **every sentence arrives at the same level of fluency regardless of the rung it came from**: an observation, a corroborated fact and an inference all read as settled narrative. The investigator editing the draft is checking whether it is *accurate*, which is a different question from whether it *climbed*. Clumsy prose exposes a leap. Good prose closes over it.

**The gaps get filled.** A model asked to write a report from incomplete notes produces a complete report, because that is what a report is. Module 2's narrative-completion mechanism, arriving at the most consequential document in the process. The sentence *"this allegation could not be resolved on the available evidence"* is the hardest sentence in this job to write, and it is the one a drafting model is least likely to generate unprompted.

**And the quality review is measuring the wrong thing.** *Better written* is Module 4's warning stated as a finding: **a more polished document is not a stronger record.** The review that rated the drafts higher was assessing the property that improved, not the property that degraded.

**B is the reference answer, and look at what it costs.** Cycle time unchanged, sometimes worse, which is why this change is almost never the one that gets funded. It is a rung-two corroboration pass, permitted at scale, verified against source documents, and it produced the only outcome on this page that speaks to whether findings hold: **no missing-evidence challenges in the matters that were actually tested.** Three matters is not evidence. It is the right kind of evidence, which is rarer.

**C is the forbidden one, and it is the one most likely to be built.** Intake classification is a rung-five determination in rung-one clothing (Module 1's central example) and a manager reviewing the classification is reviewing a conclusion. Then note the metric, because it is the most instructive error on the page: **routing consistency measures agreement, not correctness.** Two reviewers agreeing 94% of the time tells you the model is predictable. It tells you nothing about whether the matters routed to informal resolution should have been, and the person whose complaint was routed out had a right to be heard. **A rise from 71% to 94% is exactly what you would see if the model had taught both reviewers the same wrong rule.**

**D is the cheapest good change on the page, and it involves no AI at all.** It costs 1.5 days and it makes Module 4's defect structurally impossible: you cannot submit a report that leaves an allegation unaddressed. **The 19% return rate is not a problem with the template — it is the measurement of how often this was happening before anybody was checking.** Note also which change would be easiest to fund and which would be easiest to announce. They are not the same one.

The transferable test, and the module's whole argument in a question: **name the property that improved and the property that got worse. If you can only name the first, you have not finished evaluating the change.**
